# Quantum dynamics before the contour {#sec-prerequisites}

The central object of an open quantum system is a density matrix, and the central practical question is usually about a correlation function. Keldysh field theory connects these two descriptions. It turns an evolution equation for an operator into a generating functional whose derivatives produce correlations and responses. Before constructing that functional, we develop the few pieces of quantum mechanics that it uses.

These chapters follow the theoretical starting point of @Sieberer2016, with additional intermediate calculations. Throughout, $\hbar=k_B=1$. A frequency therefore has the units of an energy, and an inverse temperature has the units of a time. We use the dissipator

$$
\mathcal D[L]\rho=L\rho L^\dagger-\frac12\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}.
$$ {#eq-prereq-dissipator}

A rate multiplying this expression is a probability decay rate. The amplitude decay rate of a harmonic mode is half its particle loss rate. Keeping this distinction visible will prevent many factors of two later.

## States, mixtures, and partial traces

A pure state $|\Psi\rangle$ specifies a density matrix $\rho=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|$. A statistical mixture has the more general form

$$
\rho=\sum_r w_r |\Psi_r\rangle\langle\Psi_r|,
\qquad w_r\geq0,\qquad\sum_r w_r=1.
$$

Different ensembles can describe the same $\rho$; the density matrix is the physical object. It is Hermitian, positive, and has trace one. An observable $O$ has mean $\langle O\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(\rho O)$. Positivity means $\langle v|\rho|v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector, rather than positivity of each matrix element.

Suppose the full Hilbert space is $\mathcal H_S\otimes\mathcal H_B$. For a basis $\{|b\rangle\}$ of the bath, the reduced state is

$$
\rho_S=\operatorname{tr}_B\rho_{SB}
=\sum_b\langle b|\rho_{SB}|b\rangle.
$$

This definition follows from demanding $\operatorname{tr}_{SB}[\rho_{SB}(O_S\otimes1_B)]=\operatorname{tr}_S(\rho_S O_S)$ for every system observable. Even a pure full state generally yields a mixed reduced state. For example, tracing either spin out of $(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives $\rho_S=1/2$ on the two dimensional spin Hilbert space.

For a closed system,

$$
i\partial_t|\Psi\rangle=H|\Psi\rangle,
\qquad
\partial_t\rho=-i[H,\rho],
\qquad
\rho(t)=U(t,t_0)\rho(t_0)U^\dagger(t,t_0).
$$ {#eq-prereq-unitary-density}

The operator $U$ acts on the ket index and $U^\dagger$ on the bra index. This is the elementary reason that a real time functional integral for a density matrix needs two branches. Doubling the fields is already necessary before adding dissipation.

## What a Markovian master equation assumes

Consider $H_{SB}=H_S+H_B+\sum_\alpha A_\alpha\otimes B_\alpha$. In the interaction picture, integrating the von Neumann equation once and substituting it back produces a memory term of the form

$$
\partial_t\rho_S(t)=-\int_{t_0}^t ds\,
\operatorname{tr}_B[H_I(t),[H_I(s),\rho_{SB}(s)]],
$$

after removing an initial first order bath average. No approximation has yet made this memory term local: it depends on earlier times and on the full state.

A weak coupling derivation typically replaces $\rho_{SB}(s)$ in this kernel by $\rho_S(s)\otimes\rho_B$ and then uses the short decay time of bath correlations to replace $\rho_S(s)$ by $\rho_S(t)$ inside the memory integral. Appropriate frequency averaging is also needed to obtain a completely positive generator. The bath correlation time must be short compared with the system relaxation time. This does **not** say that every system oscillation is slow, that every bath is white at every frequency, or that a local dissipator is automatically compatible with thermal equilibrium.

The oscillator-bath calculation in @sec-worked-integrals derives the frequency dependent response and noise kernels explicitly and shows how their narrow frequency limit produces these rates.

The resulting time independent equation has the form

$$
\partial_t\rho=\mathcal L\rho
=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_\alpha\gamma_\alpha\mathcal D[L_\alpha]\rho,
\qquad\gamma_\alpha\geq0.
$$ {#eq-prereq-lindblad}

The structural theorem identifying generators of completely positive quantum dynamical semigroups is foundational [@Lindblad1976]. Here we use the displayed equation as a model whose physical derivation and regime of validity must be checked separately. Bosonic operators are unbounded; formal manipulations with them also require a sensible domain or occupation cutoff.

Trace preservation is immediate:

$$
\operatorname{tr}(L\rho L^\dagger)
=\operatorname{tr}(L^\dagger L\rho),
\qquad\operatorname{tr}\mathcal D[L]\rho=0.
$$

The positive jump term and the two anticommutator terms belong together. Removing the jump term gives a useful conditional evolution between detected jumps, but its trace decreases and it is not the unconditional master equation.

A steady state obeys $\mathcal L\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}=0$. Existence, uniqueness, and approach to it are separate questions. A finite system often has a unique stationary state; an infinite system can display phase transitions, several sectors, or persistent dynamics. Sending $t_0\to-\infty$ removes initial conditions only if the modes being studied actually relax.

## The adjoint equation and elementary diagnostics

Instead of evolving $\rho$, we may evolve observables using

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\langle O\rangle=\langle\mathcal L^\dagger O\rangle,
\quad
\mathcal L^\dagger O=i[H,O]
+\sum_\alpha\gamma_\alpha\left(L_\alpha^\dagger O L_\alpha
-\frac12\{L_\alpha^\dagger L_\alpha,O\}\right).
$$ {#eq-prereq-adjoint}

A convenient identity is

$$
\mathcal D^\dagger[L]O
=\frac12\left(L^\dagger[O,L]+[L^\dagger,O]L\right).
$$

For $[a,a^\dagger]=1$, $H=\omega_0a^\dagger a$, and loss and incoherent pump,

$$
\dot\rho=-i[\omega_0a^\dagger a,\rho]
+\kappa\mathcal D[a]\rho+p\mathcal D[a^\dagger]\rho,
$$ {#eq-prereq-cavity-master}

this identity yields

$$
\frac{d\langle a\rangle}{dt}
=-\left(i\omega_0+\frac{\kappa-p}{2}\right)\langle a\rangle,
\qquad
\frac{d\langle n\rangle}{dt}=-(\kappa-p)\langle n\rangle+p,
\quad n=a^\dagger a.
$$ {#eq-prereq-cavity-moments}

The pump contributes $p(\langle n\rangle+1)$ to particle production. The extra one is spontaneous emission into an empty mode; the term proportional to $n$ is bosonic stimulation. A stable linear stationary state requires $p<\kappa$, and then $n_{\mathrm{ss}}=p/(\kappa-p)$. If $p\geq\kappa$, saturation or other physics is needed. The failure is physical, rather than a defect in the functional integral.

More generally, a symmetry of the generator need not mean conservation of the corresponding charge. Both dissipators above are invariant under $a\mapsto e^{i\theta}a$, because phases cancel between a jump and its adjoint. Nevertheless, their particle number is not conserved. This distinction becomes essential in driven condensates.

::: {.callout-tip title="Checkpoint: rate conventions"}
For pure loss, $\langle n(t)\rangle=e^{-\kappa t}\langle n(0)\rangle$, while $\langle a(t)\rangle=e^{-(i\omega_0+\kappa/2)t}\langle a(0)\rangle$. A paper writing $2\kappa\mathcal D[a]$ has an amplitude linewidth $\kappa$; its symbol $\kappa$ denotes a different rate from ours.
:::

## Second quantization and coherent states

A bosonic occupation basis is defined by

$$
a|n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle,
\qquad
a^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle.
$$

A coherent state is particularly useful because annihilation acts by multiplication. Use the unnormalized convention

$$
|z\rangle=e^{za^\dagger}|0\rangle
=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}|n\rangle,
\qquad a|z\rangle=z|z\rangle.
$$ {#eq-prereq-coherent}

Its overlap and resolution of the identity are

$$
\langle z|w\rangle=e^{\bar z w},
\qquad
1=\int\frac{d^2z}{\pi}e^{-|z|^2}|z\rangle\langle z|,
\quad d^2z=d(\operatorname{Re}z)d(\operatorname{Im}z).
$$ {#eq-prereq-coherent-identity}

To verify completeness, insert the occupation expansion. The angular integral gives $\delta_{mn}$ and the radial integral gives $n!$, canceling the factors in the expansion. Coherent states are overcomplete, so they need not be orthogonal to resolve the identity.

A **normal ordered** polynomial has all creation operators to the left of annihilation operators. For such an operator $F_N$,

$$
\frac{\langle z|F_N(a^\dagger,a)|w\rangle}{\langle z|w\rangle}
=F_N(\bar z,w).
$$ {#eq-prereq-normal-symbol}

This is a statement about matrix elements, not an assertion that quantum operators commute. For example,

$$
aa^\dagger=a^\dagger a+1,
\quad (a^\dagger a)^2=a^{\dagger2}a^2+a^\dagger a.
$$

Their normal symbols are $\bar z w+1$ and $\bar z^2w^2+\bar z w$, respectively. Replacing $a$ by a complex number before commuting would miss these terms.

For a spatial field, $[a(\mathbf x),a^\dagger(\mathbf x')]=\delta^{(d)}(\mathbf x-\mathbf x')$. A lattice with spacing $a_0$ regulates local products, with $a_j\simeq a_0^{d/2}a(\mathbf x_j)$. Contact interactions and coincident point noise should be understood with such a regulator until physical parameters are fixed. The formal object $\delta^{(d)}(0)$ is not a measurable infinite density.

## Correlations and linear response

A density matrix determines equal time averages, but unequal time correlations require the dynamics too. In a Markovian description, for $t>t'$,

$$
\langle A(t)B(t')\rangle
=\operatorname{tr}\left[Ae^{(t-t')\mathcal L}
\bigl(B\rho(t')\bigr)\right].
$$ {#eq-prereq-regression}

This is the regression rule associated with the same system and bath approximation used for the master equation. One should not assume it for an arbitrary non-Markovian reduced state. The object being propagated, $B\rho$, need not itself be a positive density matrix; the Liouvillian acts linearly on the full operator space.

For a boson we define

$$
G^R(t,t')=-i\theta(t-t')\langle[a(t),a^\dagger(t')]\rangle,
\qquad
G^K(t,t')=-i\langle\{a(t),a^\dagger(t')\}\rangle.
$$ {#eq-prereq-green-definitions}

The commutator governs the response to a weak coherent probe. The anticommutator gives symmetrized fluctuations. At equal times,

$$
iG^K(t,t)=2\langle n(t)\rangle+1.
$$

An empty mode therefore still fluctuates. Dropping the one changes quantum vacuum noise and can give a negative occupation after converting back from symmetrized correlations.

We Fourier transform with $f(t,\mathbf x)=\int d\omega\,d^dk\,(2\pi)^{-(d+1)}e^{-i\omega t+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}f(\omega,\mathbf k)$. Thus $i\partial_t\mapsto\omega$ and $-\nabla^2\mapsto k^2$. For a stationary state, two time functions depend on $t-t'$; during heating, both times remain independent.

## Exercises with solutions

**1. Purity under mixing.** Compute $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2$ for $\rho=w|0\rangle\langle0|+(1-w)|1\rangle\langle1|$.

**Solution.** Orthogonality gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=w^2+(1-w)^2$. It equals one at the pure endpoints and reaches $1/2$ at $w=1/2$. A density matrix can be mixed even when no classical label identifying its preparation is accessible.

**2. Pair loss.** Add $\eta\mathcal D[a^2]$ to the cavity master equation. Derive its contributions to the amplitude and particle equations.

**Solution.** In the adjoint identity, $[a,a^2]=0$ and $[a^{\dagger2},a]=-2a^\dagger$, giving $\mathcal D^\dagger[a^2]a=-a^\dagger a^2$. Similarly $[n,a^2]=-2a^2$ and $[a^{\dagger2},n]=-2a^{\dagger2}$, giving $\mathcal D^\dagger[a^2]n=-2a^{\dagger2}a^2$. Thus $\dot{\langle a\rangle}|_\eta=-\eta\langle a^\dagger a^2\rangle$ and $\dot{\langle n\rangle}|_\eta=-2\eta\langle n(n-1)\rangle$. Replacing the three operator average by $|\langle a\rangle|^2\langle a\rangle$ is a mean field approximation, not an operator identity.

**3. Incoherent versus coherent pumping.** Why does $p\mathcal D[a^\dagger]$ preserve phase rotation symmetry whereas $H_f=fa^\dagger+\bar f a$ generally does not?

**Solution.** A jump may acquire a phase without changing its dissipator. A specified complex number $f$ instead selects a phase relative to which $a$ is measured. Keeping $f$ fixed while rotating $a$ changes $H_f$. This is why an incoherently pumped condensate can spontaneously choose its phase, while a resonantly driven linear cavity inherits the laser phase.
